issues.legal_issue: Entering into transactions that create interests in disputed property during an absolute restraint, and creating third-party rights without first notifying the affected parties when notice is required, breaches the court’s orders.
material_facts: An interim order prohibited the respondents from creating any interest in the disputed property.
While that restraint was in force, the respondents entered into agreements and accepted at least part of the consideration for transactions involving the property.
A later order allowed third-party rights to be created only after notice to the petitioners.
In some transactions, the respondents created third-party interests before giving notice.
issues.conclusion: The respondents breached both the absolute restraint and the later requirement to give notice before creating third-party rights.
issues.legal_principle: The terms of a clear court order govern what conduct is prohibited or permitted. The initial order prohibited creating any interest in the property, including through agreements or acceptance of consideration. The later order required notice before third-party rights were created; it did not permit notice to be given afterward.

predicates.contempt_proceeding: A proceeding seeks a finding of civil contempt for alleged noncompliance with a court order.
predicates.interest_created_during_absolute_restrai: A party entered into transactions or accepted consideration that created an interest in property while an order absolutely restraining the creation of such interests was in force.
predicates.third_party_rights_created_without_advan: A party created third-party rights in circumstances where the court had required notice beforehand, without giving that notice first.

issues.definition: In a civil contempt proceeding, an absolute restraint is breached by creating an interest while it is in force, and a notice condition is breached by creating third-party rights before giving the required notice.

issues.legal_issue: Disobedience of a clear court order known to the person bound by it is civil contempt when the person deliberately acts contrary to the order.
material_facts: The court’s orders clearly prohibited the transactions during the period of absolute restraint and required advance notice before later creation of third-party rights.
The respondents knew of the orders and entered into transactions contrary to them.
The respondents defended the transactions on the ground that the later order did not require prior notice, but the court rejected that interpretation.
issues.conclusion: The respondents’ disobedience was wilful, intentional, and deliberate, and they were guilty of civil contempt.
issues.legal_principle: Section 2(b) of the Contempt of Courts Act, 1971 defines civil contempt as wilful disobedience of a court judgment, decree, direction, order, writ, or other process, or wilful breach of an undertaking to a court. Wilfulness requires voluntary conduct with the specific intent to disobey or disregard the law. Ashok Paper Kamgar Union v. Dharam Godha explains wilful disobedience; Kapildeo Prasad Sah v. State of Bihar and Anil Ratan Sarkar v. Hirak Ghosh require a clear case of deliberate disobedience and caution that mere disobedience is insufficient. All Bengal Excise Licensees Association v. Raghabendra Singh recognizes that wilful and deliberate violation of an interim order is contempt. Tayabbhai M. Bagasarawala v. Hind Rubber Industries confirms that a party cannot escape consequences for breaching an operative interim order. Commissioner, Karnataka Housing Board v. C. Muddaiah emphasizes that a court order must be obeyed unless challenged through lawful proceedings.

predicates.civil_contempt_proceeding: A proceeding asks the court to determine whether a person has committed civil contempt.
predicates.clear_order_known_to_bound_person: The person bound by the order knew of a direction whose meaning was clear and unambiguous.
predicates.deliberate_contrary_conduct: The person voluntarily acted in a way that the known direction prohibited or failed to do what it required.

issues.definition: A person commits civil contempt when, in a civil contempt proceeding, that person knowingly and deliberately acts contrary to a clear court order.

issues.legal_issue: A tactical or insincere apology does not excuse serious deliberate contempt, and imprisonment may be imposed when a fine would not meet the ends of justice.
material_facts: The respondents tendered an unconditional apology but did so after defending their transactions and when contempt proceedings were under way.
The court found that the apology was a tactical move rather than an expression of genuine contrition.
The court considered the respondents’ deliberate violation of clear orders serious and concluded that a fine would not meet the ends of justice.
issues.conclusion: The court rejected the apology, found the respondents guilty under the applicable contempt provisions, and imposed simple imprisonment.
issues.legal_principle: Section 12 of the Contempt of Courts Act, 1971 provides for punishment for contempt and permits discharge or remission on an apology satisfactory to the court; its explanation does not require rejection of an apology merely because it is qualified or conditional if it is bona fide. Section 12(3) permits detention in civil prison when a fine will not meet the ends of justice and imprisonment is necessary. Hiren Bose, Re; M.Y. Shareaf v. Hon’ble Judges of the High Court of Nagpur; M.B. Sanghi v. High Court of Punjab & Haryana; T.N. Godavarman Thirumulpad v. Ashok Khot; and L.D. Jaikwal v. State of U.P. establish that an apology is not a defence to be used to purge guilt and must reflect genuine contrition. Article 129 of the Constitution recognizes the Supreme Court’s power to punish contempt of itself; Section 94(c) and Order XXXIX Rule 2A of the Code of Civil Procedure address disobedience of interim orders and its consequences.

rule.if: civil_contempt_proceeding and serious_deliberate_breach and apology_not_genuine and fine_insufficient

predicates.civil_contempt_proceeding: A proceeding asks the court to punish a person for civil contempt.
predicates.serious_deliberate_breach: The person knowingly and deliberately commits a serious breach of a court order.
predicates.apology_not_genuine: The apology is not a genuine expression of contrition and is instead offered as a tactic to avoid consequences.
predicates.fine_insufficient: The court determines that a fine would not adequately serve the ends of justice.

issues.definition: In a civil contempt proceeding, a serious deliberate breach accompanied by an insincere apology and a finding that a fine is insufficient results in rejection of the apology and imprisonment.
